analysis.title: US Midterm Elections: what to expect and what the market impact could be
key_insights: Crédit Agricole CIB handicaps the 3 November midterms at Democratic sweep 65%, Democratic House/Republican Senate 25%, Republican sweep 10%. Republican House/Democratic Senate is called highly unlikely.
Trump's overall approval is below 40%, more than 20ppt underwater. Net approval is -32.4ppt on the economy, -43.8ppt on inflation and -10.6ppt on immigration.

The House: Republicans hold 220-215 (vacancies assigned to prior holder), so Democrats need a net gain of at least 3 seats. The generic ballot favours Democrats by more than 8ppt, a swing of close to 11ppt from the 2024 House vote that Republicans won by 2.6ppt. The bank puts odds of a Democratic House at around 90%.
Redistricting has limited the seats truly in play to the 20s, so a wave of 40+ seats is highly unlikely.

The Senate is a closer call. Republicans hold 53-47, Democrats need a net gain of 4 seats (a 50-50 tie is broken by VP Vance), and the bank puts Democratic odds at around 65%. Seats rated toss-up by Cook include Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.

With a Democratic House, legislative gridlock is likely whichever party holds the Senate, because of the filibuster and the presidential veto. A Senate win would matter mainly for judicial and other appointments and for oversight. Impeachment is seen as noise, since removal needs two-thirds of the Senate.

A government shutdown is possible either way, and the bank sees a decent chance of another one next year. Tariffs and foreign policy are not expected to change much because they rest on presidential authority.

Rates: a divided government reduces the odds of major spending programmes and tax cuts, easing term premium and long-end yields. That is supportive of lower long-end yields and a flatter curve. Front-end yields stay high because of elevated energy prices and further expected Fed hikes.

The FY2026 federal deficit was USD1.99trn (about 6% of GDP), on USD7.4trn of spending (+6%) and USD5.4trn of revenue (+3%). The prior two years were USD1.775trn (FY2025) and USD1.817trn (FY2024). CBO projects debt-to-GDP rising from 100% to 120% within a decade.
Forecasts: 2Y 4.75% in Dec-26 and 4.60% in Dec-27. 10Y 5.05% in Dec-26 and 4.95% in Dec-27. 30Y 5.40% in Dec-26 and 5.30% in Dec-27.

FX: market betting odds point to a Democratic sweep. Since 1976 a Democratic Congress with a GOP president has coincided with USD weakness in the months after the vote, while a GOP president and Senate with a Democratic House has coincided with USD gains (last seen after 2018, with a hawkish Fed and a recovering economy).

The bank's main FX scenario is cyclical convergence between the US and the rest of G10: slowing AI investment, fading US fiscal support, lower energy costs, fiscal support in Europe and Japan, and Fed rate cuts in H2 2027. The risk scenarios are an AI boom-bust, a persistent energy shock, and US or global recession or stagflation.

Emerging markets: the midterms are not seen as a game changer. Three issues matter: fiscal and growth, Iran and oil, and the AI trade. Trump could become more or less assertive on Iran, so the effect on oil is unclear.

EM data: exports are accelerating (electronics and chips in Asia, commodity prices in Latin America and the Middle East), industrial production and retail sales are resilient outside China, and China's 2026 GDP growth is expected at 4.6%. The EM-DM carry gap is about 311bp, in the 'decently attractive' range.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Exceptionally large for a period without recession, which keeps pressure on term premium.
Front-end yields stay high because of elevated energy prices and expected further Fed hikes.
Gridlock is expected to ease term premium, so long-end yields drift lower later in the forecast.
Supports a flatter curve as long-end yields ease.
Debt accumulation cannot be reversed by growth alone.
Growth is supported by targeted stimulus and exports.

risk_factors: Legislative gridlock and possible government shutdowns next year
An AI boom-bust cycle triggering a global market selloff
A persistent negative energy shock hurting global growth
A US or global recession or stagflation
Trump becoming more assertive on Iran, pushing oil higher
Elevated deficits (about 6% of GDP) and rising debt pushing up term premium

vol_and_positioning: Market betting odds point to Democrats winning both the House and the Senate.
Foreign investors have been buying US stocks but not Treasuries.
geopolitical: US midterm elections on 3 November 2026 and their effect on Trump's foreign policy leeway.
Iran: a Democratic Congress could limit funding for Trump's assertiveness, or Trump could become more assertive to galvanise his base, with oil price effects either way.
US-China: bipartisan consensus on the need to cap China's geoeconomic ascent, so the midterms are not a game changer.
Tariffs and trade rest on authority delegated to the president, so Congress is unlikely to change them.

tension_points.bull_case: A Democratic Congress with a GOP president has coincided with USD weakness in the months after the vote since 1976, and gridlock and fading fiscal support point to cyclical convergence and a weaker USD.
tension_points.bear_case: A GOP president and Senate with a Democratic House has coincided with a broad USD rally, as after the 2018 midterms with a recovering economy and a hawkish Fed.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An AI boom-bust and risk aversion spike, or US growth outperformance with a hawkish Fed, would move the USD away from the convergence scenario.

tension_points.bull_case: Divided government reduces the likelihood of major spending programmes and tax cuts, easing term premium and long-end yields and flattening the curve.
tension_points.bear_case: The deficit is about 6% of GDP, debt-to-GDP is heading to 120%, and front-end yields stay high with elevated energy prices and further Fed hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Republican sweep, or a deficit path that keeps widening, would remove the term premium relief.
